exercises.heading: Section 7.9 Exercises
exercises.paragraph: For the following exercises, we are considering a special 6-sided die, with faces that are labeled with a number and a letter: 1A, 1B, 2A, 2C, 4A, and 4E. You are about to roll this die twice.

problem.paragraph: What is the probability of rolling two 1s?
What is the probability of rolling two vowels?
What is the probability of rolling an even number first and an odd number second?
What is the probability of rolling an even number and an odd number in any order?
What is the probability of rolling a consonant first and a 1 second?
What is the probability of rolling one number less than 3 and one number greater than 3, in any order?

exercises.paragraph: In the following exercises, you are about to draw Scrabble tiles from a bag; the bag contains the letters A, A, C, E, E, E, L, L, N, O, R, S, S, S, T, X.

problem.paragraph: If you draw 1 tile at random, compute $$P\left( \text{tile shows A} \right)$$ $$P\left( \text{tile shows A} | \text{tile shows a vowel} \right)$$
If you draw 1 tile at random, compute: $$P( \text{tile shows a vowel} )$$ $$P\left( \text{tile shows a vowel} | \text{tile shows a letter that comes after M alphabetically} \right)$$
If you draw 2 tiles with replacement, compute $$P( \text{both are vowels} )$$ .
If you draw 2 tiles without replacement, compute $$P( \text{both are vowels} )$$ .
If you draw 2 tiles with replacement, compute $$P( \text{first is a vowel and second is a consonant} )$$ .
If you draw 2 tiles without replacement, compute $$P( \text{first is a vowel and second is a consonant} )$$ .
If you draw 2 tiles with replacement, compute $$P( \text{one is a vowel and one is a consonant} )$$ .
If you draw 2 tiles without replacement, compute $$P( \text{one is a vowel and one is a consonant} )$$ .
If you draw 2 tiles with replacement, compute $$P( \text{both are Es} )$$ .
If you draw 2 tiles without replacement, compute $$P( \text{both are Es} )$$ .

exercises.paragraph: For the following exercises, use the table provided, which breaks down the enrollment at a certain liberal arts college by class year and area of study. Class Year First-Year Sophomore Junior Senior Totals Area Of Study Arts 138 121 148 132 539 Humanities 258 301 275 283 1117 Social Science 142 151 130 132 555 Natural Science/Mathematics 175 197 203 188 763 Totals 713 770 756 735 2974

problem.paragraph: Compute the probability that a randomly selected student is a sophomore, given that they are majoring in the arts.
Compute the probability that a randomly selected student is majoring in the arts, given that they are a sophomore.
If two seniors are chosen at random, compute the probability that both are social science majors. Give your answer as a decimal, rounded to 5 decimal places.
If two humanities majors are chosen at random, compute the probability that the first is a senior and the second is a junior. Give your answer as a decimal, rounded to 5 decimal places.

If two natural science/mathematics majors are chosen at random, compute the probability that one is a sophomore and one is a senior (in any order). Give your answer as a decimal, rounded to 5 decimal places.
If two students are chosen at random, compute the probability that one is an arts major and one is a social science major, in any order. Give your answer as a decimal, rounded to 5 decimal places.

exercises.paragraph: In the following exercises deal with the game “Punch a Bunch,” which appears on the TV game show The Price Is Right. In this game, contestants have a chance to punch through up to 4 paper circles on a board; behind each circle is a card with a dollar amount printed on it. There are 50 of these circles; the dollar amounts are given in this table: Dollar Amount Frequency \$25,000 1 \$10,000 2 \$5,000 4 \$2,500 8 \$1,000 10 \$500 10 \$250 10 \$100 5 Contestants are shown their selected dollar amounts one at a time, in the order selected. After each is revealed, the contestant is given the option of taking that amount of money or throwing it away in favor of the next amount. (You can watch the game being played in the video Playing “Punch a Bunch.”) Jeremy is playing “Punch a Bunch” and gets 2 punches.

problem.paragraph: What is the probability that both punches are worth less than \$1,000?
What is the probability that both punches are worth more than \$2,500?
What is the probability that the second punch is worth more than the first punch, given that the first punch was worth \$250?
What is the probability that the second punch is worth more than the first punch, given that the first punch was worth \$1,000?
What is the probability that the second punch is worth less than the first punch, given that the first punch was worth \$250?
What is the probability that the second punch is worth less than the first punch, given that the first punch was worth \$1,000?
What is the probability that both punches are worth \$100?
What is the probability that both punches are worth the same amount?

exercises.paragraph: In the following exercises, we consider two baseball teams playing a best-of-three series (meaning the first team to win two games wins the series). Team A is a little bit better than Team B, so we expect Team A will win 55% of the time.

problem.paragraph: What is the probability that Team A wins the series given that Team B wins the first game?
What is the probability that Team B wins the series given that Team B wins the first game?
What is the probability that Team B wins the series given that Team A wins the first game?
What is the probability that Team A wins the series given that Team A wins the first game?
Build a tree diagram that shows all possible outcomes of the series. Label the edges with appropriate probabilities.
What is the probability that Team A wins the series?
If instead Team A has a 75% chance of winning each game, what is the probability that Team A wins the series?
If instead Team A has a 90% chance of winning each game, what is the probability that Team A wins the series?
